item.title: Specific, cumulative and reversible odour learning in a whole-brain connectome model of Drosophila
item.description: arXiv:2611.09930v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Whole-brain models of the fruit fly built from the FlyWire connectome can predict how neurons respond to a stimulus, but they keep every synapse fixed and so cannot learn, while models that do learn simulate only the mushroom body. I made the synapses from Kenyon cells (KCs) to mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) plastic in a whole-brain leaky integrate-and-fire model of the FlyWire connectome, under a rule in which dopamine weakens each synapse in proportion to how strongly its KC fired. Odours reached the KCs through the connectome's mapped olfactory wiring, and punishment was delivered by driving the 12 PPL1 dopamine neurons at 100 Hz. Pairing an odour with punishment lowered the response of approach MBONs to that odour from 11.3 to 0.3 Hz in all five noise replicates of one simulated brain, while unpaired and never-paired odours and controls with the rule switched off or scrambled changed little. A second odour paired on the already trained brain was learned at 85.5% of the strength reached by a naive brain, and approach MBONs ended with weak responses to both odours. With a timing rule in which dopamine arriving before the odour strengthens a synapse, a simulated fly body driven by the model unlearned and relearned in four of four cycles, whereas the first rule got stuck after one; backward pairing alone was too weak to reach behaviour. All results are for aversive learning; reward learning could not be tested because, at the synaptic weight and synapse floor used here, sugar input does not recruit the reward dopamine neurons. Learning depended on an authored plasticity rule, an injected punishment signal and other authored choices detailed in Methods; given these choices, the odour-specificity of learning followed from the structure of the connectome.
item.dc:creator: Daniel F. Asis

item.title: Pixels over Symbols: Sensory Realism Improves Behavioral Alignment in Models of Cognition
item.description: arXiv:2611.10565v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computational models of cognition have traditionally relied on abstract symbolic inputs that approximate sensory experiences with simplified vector representations. This simplification reflects historical computational constraints and a long-held assumption that the details of sensory realism are incidental to the study of cognitive processes. Recent advances have enabled the development of sensory-realistic models capable of performing diverse cognitive tasks, yet whether sensory realism meaningfully shapes cognition has not been formally established. We address this gap through a large-scale empirical comparison of abstract and sensory-realistic neural network models trained on a battery of memory-dependent decision-making tasks. Our results show that sensory-realistic models mirror human behavioral response patterns significantly more than their abstract counterparts, though a substantial gap to human internal behavioral consistency remains even for the best tested models. By analyzing the internal dynamics of these systems, we find that the learned recurrent weights are not the main source of this divergence. In fact, frozen abstract-trained weights driven by sensory-realistic inputs recover the human consistency of sensory-realistic models. The resulting dynamics are also within the seed-to-seed variability of sensory-realistic models. Together, our findings argue that across a broad set of visual working-memory tasks, sensory realism accounts for a substantial portion of the model-human behavioral agreement, more than the choice of sequence architecture and comparable to the choice of vision encoder. These results suggest that findings obtained from abstract task models in neuroscience should be more carefully interpreted in light of their potential behavioral limitations.
item.dc:creator: Hao Yuan Bai, Xiaoxuan Lei, Zihan Weng, Motahareh Pourrahimi, Lucas Gomez, Pouya Bashivan

item.title: NeuroHorizon: Long-Horizon Forecasting of Neural Population Activity with Hierarchical Memory
item.description: arXiv:2611.10617v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon forecasting of neural population activity tests whether a model has captured dynamics that remain predictive well beyond the observed history. Prediction quality typically declines as the horizon grows, yet neither short-horizon accuracy nor teacher-forced evaluation, which supplies the true activity preceding each predicted step, reveals how well models sustain predictions from an initial history alone. We compare direct multi-step prediction and autoregressive rollout on spiking recordings across horizons and introduce NeuroHorizon, which pairs event-based spike encoding with a causal decoder for population firing rates. Its hierarchical prediction memory keeps recent predictions at full temporal resolution and compresses earlier ones into segment summaries, giving the decoder both local detail and longer-range context. Under teacher-forced training this memory holds ground-truth activity, whereas during rollout it holds the model's own predictions. To reduce this mismatch, we train with scheduled sampling, progressively exposing the decoder to its own predictions. From 500 ms of macaque motor-cortex activity, NeuroHorizon achieves the highest forward-prediction score among the evaluated autonomous models at all four horizons from 100 to 1000 ms, and its per-bin predictions remain above a mean-firing-rate baseline across nearly the full 1 s window. Complementary experiments on macaque sensorimotor and mouse multi-region recordings show that performance generally increases with model and data size, alongside improved prediction after cross-subject pretraining and fine-tuning. Together, these results clarify how forecasting performance changes across horizons and offer an effective approach to long-horizon forecasting of neural population activity.
item.dc:creator: Peng Jiang, Xiaoxuan Jia

item.title: From MNH to the Friedman--Komogortsev Method---which changes improve eye-movement classification?
item.description: arXiv:2611.11519v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Friedman-Komogortsev Method (FKM) is a rule-based classifier of fixations, saccades, and post-saccadic oscillations in 1000-Hz recordings, developed from the modified Nystr\"om-Holmqvist algorithm (MNH) and used in several recent studies. FKM changes MNH in many ways at once: it centres MNH's Savitzky-Golay filter, adds a position-based test for whether an apparent post-saccadic oscillation continues the saccade, adds rejection tests, and changes several thresholds. We asked which of these changes alter agreement with human classification. Both algorithms were scored against twenty 26-s GazeBase reading recordings hand-classified by three trained raters, and each change was reverted in turn. FKM agreed better than MNH as MNH was used: saccade Cohen's kappa rose on all 20 recordings (median +0.034), and saccade boundaries moved from 2-3 ms late to the raters' sample. One change produced this: centring the filter, which removes a three-sample delay. Reinstating the delay returned FKM's saccade kappa to MNH's value, and centring MNH's filter alone made MNH match FKM on saccades and exceed it on post-saccadic events. The position-based test changed how saccades with several velocity peaks were divided, splitting 8% of rater-labelled "wavy" saccades into a saccade and a spurious oscillation against 39% for delay-corrected MNH. FKM's higher post-saccadic velocity floor traded recall for precision. The remaining changes had no measurable effect on these recordings. FKM's improvement over MNH is therefore a filter-alignment correction that MNH users can apply directly, plus a segmentation rule for multi-peak saccades.
item.dc:creator: Lee Friedman, Mehedi Hasan Raju, Oleg Komogortsev

item.title: Language processing in the autistic brain: A meta-analysis of neuroimaging studies across modalities and age
item.description: arXiv:2611.11927v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language is central to social communication, which is altered in autism, and language abilities vary widely among autistic individuals. How the autistic brain processes language is central to understanding autistic communication. Yet neuroimaging studies report inconsistent findings on how autistic brain activity is altered during language processing. We synthesized 45 fMRI and PET studies (753 autistic and 777 non-autistic participants) with seed-based d mapping with permutation of subject images (SDM-PSI). We estimated autistic and non-autistic activation and their difference with meta-regressions adjusted for each study's language modality and mean age. Autistic and non-autistic brains activated a similar left-lateralized language network. Autistic brains showed reduced activity throughout the left perisylvian cortex, from the inferior frontal gyrus to the mid superior temporal gyrus and the posterior superior temporal sulcus, and increased activity in the right temporal pole. Spoken language showed a larger autistic reduction than written language in the left mid superior temporal gyrus. Adults, but not children and adolescents, showed increased autistic activity in the right superior temporal gyrus and cuneus. Autistic language processing thus relies on the typical left-lateralized network but shows reduced leftward lateralization.
item.dc:creator: Hanlin Wu, Bei Xiao, Qingxi He

item.title: Spike-to-Field Mechanisms of Turbulence-Like Dynamics in Spatial Spiking Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.12627v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural avalanches and turbulence-like brain dynamics are usually measured after neural activity has been coarse-grained into continuous fields, leaving open which spike-level mechanisms can generate these macroscopic observables. We build a spatial leaky integrate-and-fire spiking neural network and explicitly transform spikes into activity-density and Hilbert phase fields. A delayed, distance-dependent, passive-dendrite regime reproducibly generates turbulence-like field structure, including high-amplitude phase-defect tracks, structure-function scaling, and power-law-favored continuous-field avalanche tails. Controls show that firing rate, vortex count, and avalanche tail fits are individually insufficient: destroying delayed propagation, dendritic filtering, or spike timing suppresses key field signatures, while random-space nulls can retain many mathematical phase defects but show weaker spatial structure and synaptic-delay transfer. Biologically motivated gates further shape the regime: PV-like perisomatic inhibition clamps phase dynamics, SST-like dendritic inhibition and projection-specific inhibitory facilitation preserve long-lived tracks, and a rate-constrained projection-STP regime expresses a roughly 200-ms episode at 12.25 Hz (full-record mean) across 12 seeds. These results use SNNs as a mechanistic testbed for spike-derived brain turbulence observables and show why phase defects and avalanche-like statistics must be interpreted jointly with spatial scaling and spike-level propagation.
item.dc:creator: Zequan Liu

item.title: Qualiaphobic artificial neural networks (and why to build them)
item.description: arXiv:2611.12809v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper introduces qualiaphobic AI: artificial neural network architectures that are hostile to theories of consciousness. I show that qualiaphobia can be well-justified by knowledge about theories of consciousness, like when such theories are trivial or unfalsifiable or contradicted by overwhelming scientific evidence. It can also be justified by how theories of consciousness must be grounded in phenomenology, as well as how current popular theories of consciousness are applied to AI. I identify and explore three convergent ways of engineering qualiaphobia that would minimize the potential for artificial consciousness. These include making AI architectures as close as possible to "anchor points" of systems with minimal potential for consciousness, fragmenting any potential phenomenology AI might have, and designing artificial neural networks in a way adversarial to popular theories of consciousness. In particular, I develop one "anchor point" of minimal potential for consciousness: systems where only behaviorist theories of consciousness can apply, and I propose qualiaphobic transformations that move existing artificial neural networks toward such systems. Additionally, I develop an account of how AIs can form justified beliefs about their own non-consciousness (or minimal potential for consciousness) and expand on how this knowledge would change their behavior. Most critically, I begin with why this research is important: qualiaphobic AI has epistemic properties that make it far better aligned with human civilization. Since consciousness is central to moral value, a world in which AIs are non-conscious ensures it is always morally correct for AI to assist and serve humanity, rather than pursue its own ends.
item.dc:creator: Erik Hoel

item.title: Memory flows: geometry and dynamics of sequential retrieval in input-driven Hopfield networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.09995v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Associative memory models classically describe retrieval as convergence to stored patterns, but the theory of sequential retrieval remains comparatively limited. We develop a two-timescale input-driven Hopfield network in which fast associative retrieval is modulated by a slow feedback variable evolving over a prescribed memory-transition graph. This yields autonomous, graph-constrained transitions while preserving analytical tractability. Using slow-fast and geometric singular perturbation theory, we characterize memory fixation via memory manifolds and identify the geometric regions that govern stability loss and escape from retrieved memories. We further derive reduced slow dynamics and explicit criteria for transition onset, self-sustained retrieval, and collapse, expressed through escape times, gain thresholds, and fixed points. Together, these results provide a tractable framework for analyzing feedback-driven sequential retrieval in Hopfield networks.
item.dc:creator: Simone Betteti, Matteo Martin, Morten Gram Pedersen, Sandro Zampieri, Giacomo Baggio

item.title: Perception, Not Reasoning, Limits Visual Theory of Mind
item.description: arXiv:2611.10694v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language models pass text-based false-belief probes at near-human levels but drop by over twenty percentage points on abstract panels the moment the same problem is conveyed visually. The consensus diagnosis is conceptual, prescribing new belief-reasoning modules. We argue the dominant bottleneck is perceptual: not what the model cannot reason about, but what it cannot see. We propose a five-condition dissociation protocol that holds the reasoning task constant while varying perceptual fidelity from visual only to text only, and quantify the result with the Perceptual Contribution Ratio, the share of the visual-to-text gap a given fidelity closes. We test this on two kinds of scenes: abstract 2D panels in the Heider--Simmel tradition, and naturalistic 3D game scenes from MuMA-ToM and MindPower. The evaluation covers seven VLMs and roughly 159,000 API calls. Ground-truth scaffolds substantially close the gap in every setting, and on the abstract panels and MuMA-ToM they match or exceed the text-only reasoning. Whereas scaffolds built by automatic parsers, including frontier VLMs, fail. The most common error in the visual-only condition is \emph{reality bias}, which accounts for 60\% of false-belief failures. Models report where an object actually is, not where an absent agent believes it is. This points to a perceptual front-end that fails to track which agents were present at each moment. Under the evaluated protocol, structured visual scene-state extraction, rather than belief inference, is the dominant bottleneck for visual ToM.
item.dc:creator: Mohamed Rayan Barhdadi, Syed Talal Wasim, Juergen Gall, Erchin Serpedin, Hasan Kurban

item.title: Learning Actionable Information Landscapes for Multimodal Active Sensing in Hawkmoths
item.description: arXiv:2611.11011v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Animals integrate information across sensory modalities to guide exploration, suggesting that they maintain internal estimates of where actions are expected to reduce uncertainty. However, how such action-conditioned information maps are learned from multimodal sensory experience remains unclear, as previous studies have been largely confined to unimodal sensing frameworks. We introduce a multimodal predictive-coding framework for learning uncertainty-reduction maps from visual and mechanosensory observations in hawkmoth flower interaction tasks. A variational generative model trained on simulated environments recovers modality-specific information landscapes over the action space, capturing how visual patterns, surface geometry, and mechanosensory cues shape the value of exploratory actions. These learned maps are consistent with several features of hawkmoth behavior, including nonzero tracking offsets, probing along visual patterns, and geometry-dependent exploration. Applying the model to behavioral data from flower tracking and nectary search, we find that natural trajectories tend to occupy regions of high uncertainty reduction in these learned maps. Building on these observations, we develop an uncertainty-gated lexicographic algorithm that switches between information gathering and reward exploitation based on perceptual uncertainty. In nectary search, uncertainty gating improves learning relative to exploit-only, $\epsilon$-greedy, fixed-time, and uncertainty-calibrated non-lexicographic controls, with better generalization and robustness to sensory and curvature shifts. These results link information landscapes learned through generative modeling to biological sensing and embodied exploration.
item.dc:creator: Abdelrahman Sharafeldin, Yaqing Wang, Simon Sponberg, Hannah Choi

item.title: MICE: Multi-animal Interaction Context Encoder - A Hierarchical Foundation Model for Mouse Behavior
item.description: arXiv:2611.11644v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantifying mouse behavior from pose is a foundational tool in neuroscience, ethology, drug discovery, and animal welfare. Self-supervised foundation models are a natural fit, but a foundation model for mouse behavior must handle social behavior - many behaviors that matter (aggression, courtship, mounting, allogrooming) are inherently multi-animal. Existing self-supervised pose models fall short: they encode each animal independently and discard interaction signal, hard-code the animal count, and pretrain one dataset at a time. We introduce MICE (Multi-animal Interaction Context Encoder), a hierarchical foundation model for mouse behavior that pretrains jointly on six mouse-pose corpora spanning one to four mice and 7 to 27 keypoints. MICE combines a hierarchical individual encoder capturing per-mouse kinematics at multiple temporal scales with a Perceiver-style social encoder whose learned latent codebook decouples parameter count from animal count, so a single checkpoint serves any group size without retraining. Across four evaluation protocols spanning six datasets, MICE matches or exceeds prior keypoint-based baselines, and layer-wise probing shows the social stage incrementally improves discriminability beyond the individual encoder. Code, weights, and data are available at https://github.com/eric0708/MICE.
item.dc:creator: Yen-Shuo Su, Weihan Li, Anqi Wu

item.title: TrajLift: Lifting Memory Recall Trajectories with Latency-Modulated Heat Diffusion
item.description: arXiv:2611.12197v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Verbal memory retrieval carries rich diagnostic information for Alzheimer's disease through the order, hesitation, and categorical organization of recalled words, yet computational modeling of this retrieval process remains largely unexplored. A key challenge is that timing and hierarchical structure are diagnostically entangled: the diagnostic meaning of retrieval timing depends on its hierarchical context. We propose TrajLift, a spectral framework that models verbal recall as timed trajectories on a hierarchical graph. Our central mechanism is latency-modulated heat diffusion on the semantic hierarchy, a unified operator that lifts each recalled word into a representation of both multi-scale hierarchical structure and continuous retrieval timing. Formal analysis shows that the resulting representation is first-order separable into structural and temporal components with spectral selectivity across hierarchical levels. On synthetic benchmarks requiring structure-time interaction, TrajLift stays near-perfect on deep hierarchies where all baselines fail. On real-world clinical data, we show that TrajLift outperforms diverse baselines by jointly modeling timing and semantic structure, with gains that grow as retrieval timing becomes more informative.
item.dc:creator: Jiawen Kang, Jinchao Li, Mingyu Cui, Junan Li, Xixin Wu, Helen Meng

item.title: K-prop: Deep Online Learning by Backpropagating Temporal Kernels
item.description: arXiv:2611.12530v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Self-recurrence represents an important component for temporal processing in neural networks, both artificial and biological, where it appears naturally in the form of leaky integration. However, due to the complex temporal dependencies of the gradient, an efficient and effective method of online training is still lacking. Here we propose K-prop, a novel online learning method for leaky neural networks. It dramatically reduces the computational and memory cost of real time recurrent learning (RTRL) by propagating kernel gains. K-prop also outperforms existing RTRL approximations and achieves performance comparable to backpropagation through time in sequence learning, classification, and reinforcement learning tasks. We further analyze how its sole approximation affects gradient quality and identify conditions under which K-prop remains accurate and effective.
item.dc:creator: Bingkun Liu, Paul Haider, Federico Benitez, Mihai A. Petrovici, Walter Senn

item.title: Burstiness and interpersonal foraging between human infants and caregivers in the vocal domain
item.description: arXiv:2505.01545v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Adult caregiver vocal responses are believed to promote more frequent and more advanced infant vocalizations. However, the inherent hierarchical temporal clustering of infant and caregiver vocal interactions over the course of a day creates a confound for reliably measuring immediate turn-by-turn effects of social vocal input within real-world vocal behavior. We first quantify temporal clustering in infant and caregiver vocalization events in daylong naturalistic infant-centered (ages 3, 6, 9, and 18 months) audio recordings using positive correlations between successive inter-event intervals (IEIs). Informed by flight time analyses in foraging studies, we develop an analytical framework to assess the effect of social input on the timing of subsequent infant and caregiver vocalizations after controlling for endogenous temporal dynamics as quantified by positive IEI-to-IEI correlations. For both infants and adults, receiving a social response predicts a shorter subsequent inter-event interval (IEI) than would be expected in the absence of a response. These results support a conceptualization of infant-caregiver vocal interactions as an `interpersonal foraging' process with inherent multiscale dynamics wherein social responses serve as foraged-for resources. The analytic approaches introduced here offer a broadly applicable framework to study interactive communication in other modalities, contexts, and species by decoupling endogenous and exogenous dynamics.
item.dc:creator: VPS Ritwika, Sara Schneider, Lukas D. Lopez, Jeffrey Mai, Ajay Gopinathan, Christopher T. Kello, Anne S. Warlaumont

item.title: Characterizing sleep stages through the complexity--weighted-entropy plane in human intracranial data and in a whole-brain model
item.description: arXiv:2511.09243v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Approaches based on symbolic information, such as entropy and complexity, have shown that sleep reorganizes the temporal structure of brain activity. However, most of this evidence comes from scalp EEG and group averages. In this work, we characterized sleep stages in intracranial recordings from 65 patients during wakefulness and the REM, N2, and N3 stages, using weighted permutation entropy (WPE) and the statistical complexity measure (SCM). In the complexity--entropy plane, the states formed a clear trajectory from wakefulness to REM, N2, and N3, with decreasing entropy and increasing complexity as sleep deepened. This organization was observed individually in most patients and was recovered more consistently by WPE than by conventional permutation entropy. The trajectory, however, was not the same throughout the cortex. All regions shifted in the same direction, but the occipital cortex followed a much shorter path than the parietal cortex. This result reflects the spatial heterogeneity of the brain during sleep and shows that cortical regions differ not only in the position they occupy in the plane, but also in the path they follow between states. Finally, a whole-brain model based on the human connectome showed that increasing neuronal adaptation shifts the simulated dynamics in the same direction observed in the empirical data, pointing to adaptation as one of the candidate mechanisms involved in this reorganization.
item.dc:creator: Helena Bordini de Lucas, Leonardo Dalla Porta, Alain Destexhe, Maria V. Sanchez-Vives, Osvaldo A. Rosso, Cl\'audio R. Mirasso, Fernanda Selingardi Matias

item.title: Scaling signatures of near-critical dynamics in large-scale human resting-state electrophysiology
item.description: arXiv:2602.17820v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: From 1/f noise to neuronal avalanches, evidence of scaling in brain activity has been increasingly linked to tuning to or near criticality. The concept of scaling is intimately related to the renormalization group (RG), in essence providing coarse-grained, simplified descriptions that generalize to classes of diverse physical systems. Following the RG idea, scaling laws have been reported in populations of spiking neurons at microscopic scales. Whether similar scaling principles govern large-scale neural activity in the human brain and how they relate to underlying neural physiology remains unresolved. Here, we analyze large-scale electrophysiological recordings (MEG) of human resting-state brain activity and apply a RG-inspired coarse-graining approach to track collective neural dynamics across spatial scales. We find that multiple observables exhibit robust scale-invariant behavior under coarse-graining: activity variance and correlations grow according to power laws, covariance eigenspectra follow a characteristic scaling relation, and neuronal avalanche statistics and scaling relationships are conserved. Using an analytically tractable neural network model with parameters inferred from data, we show that the observed scaling signatures arise close to, but slightly below, criticality, and that the scaling exponents can be modulated by network inhibitory drives. These findings demonstrate that RG-inspired scaling analysis can uncover signatures of critical dynamics in non-invasive human electrophysiology and suggest a principled route toward estimating excitation-inhibition balance from large-scale brain recordings.
item.dc:creator: Irem Topal, Anna Poggialini, Marco Dal Maschio, Daniele De Martino, Oren Shriki, Fabrizio Lombardi

item.title: INTENSE: Information-theoretic discovery of behavioral selectivity of neurons in calcium imaging data
item.description: arXiv:2603.04622v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Neurons in freely behaving animals exhibit selectivity for diverse variables. Calcium imaging makes this selectivity hard to read out: behavioral variables covary, and fluorescence is slow and autocorrelated. We introduce INTENSE (INformation-Theoretic Evaluation of Neuronal SElectivity), an open-source framework that screens every neuron against all measured variables on a common statistical scale. INTENSE applies mutual information directly to fluorescence to detect relationships missed by linear correlation, optimizes neural-behavioral delays, performs autocorrelation-preserving circular-shift tests and examines whether apparent mixed selectivity reflects behavioral covariance. In ground-truth simulations, it reduced false associations caused by temporal structure and recovered more true associations than correlation-based screening. In CA1 recordings from 16 freely exploring mice, INTENSE identified neurons selective for position, head direction, object interaction and locomotor state. Accounting for correlated variables reclassified a large fraction of apparently mixed-selective neuron-session observations. INTENSE turns neural and behavioral recordings into testable maps of neuronal selectivity.
item.dc:creator: Nikita Pospelov, Viktor Plusnin, Olga Rogozhnikova, Anna Ivanova, Vladimir Sotskov, Ksenia Toropova, Olga Ivashkina, Vladik Avetisov, Konstantin Anokhin

item.title: On Agentic Behavioral Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2604.27894v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Integrating theoretical neuroscience, decision theory, and probabilistic inference offers a promising route to understanding human cognition, yet concrete methodological bridges between agentic artificial intelligence (AI) models and behavioral data analysis remain formally underdeveloped. We advance this synthesis within the framework of agentic behavioral modeling (ABM), which treats artificial agents as latent, generative hypotheses about cognitive mechanisms and evaluates them by their statistical adequacy in explaining human behavior. After outlining its conceptual foundations, we apply the framework to two minimal laboratory paradigms: a binary perceptual contrast-discrimination task and a symmetric two-armed bandit learning task. We formalize each task-agent-data system as a joint probability model, derive explicit conditional log-likelihoods for behavioral inference, validate different model variants using model and parameter recovery simulations, and evaluate them in light of empirical data. Using these minimal examples, we provide a novel agent-centric interpretation of the psychometric function, derive optimal policies for both tasks under explicit assumptions on sensory bias and post-decision noise, and show that the Bayesian posterior expectation and induced decisions admit an equivalent adaptive-rate Rescorla-Wagner representation in the symmetric bandit task. More broadly, this work may serve as a conceptual and practical foundation for applying ABM to cognitive behavioral science.
item.dc:creator: Dirk Ostwald, Rasmus Bruckner, Franziska Us\'ee, Belinda Fleischmann, Joram Soch, Sean Mulready

item.title: Mechanistic bridges from receptors to whole-brain dynamics: promise and limits of master-equation mean-field models
item.description: arXiv:2608.00306v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Drug and disease perturbations often arise at molecular, synaptic or cellular scales, yet are often observed in population and whole-brain signals. Which microscopic mechanisms stay explicit, interpretable and testable through tractable reductions, and what can whole-brain models claim? We follow the master-equation lineage of receptor-aware adaptive mean fields, from finite-size statistics and semi-analytical transfer functions to connectome-coupled conductance-based adaptive nodes. Re-deriving its moment equations, we correct the covariance equation, which omitted a curvature term of the same order as those kept. We compare this strategy with phenomenological neural masses, exact low-dimensional and population-density reductions, large-scale spiking models and learned or hybrid surrogates. We find that effective excitatory/inhibitory synaptic kinetics, conductance state and spike-frequency adaptation can stay manipulable across scales, enabling interpretable, pharmacology-informed perturbations with testable meso- and macroscopic effects. Yet this requires coarse-grained Markovianity, population homogeneity, quasi-stationary transfer functions, moment closure, regional uniformity and measurement-specific observation models. Moreover, first-order whole-brain models discard covariance dynamics, and macroscopic fits do not identify a unique molecular cause. In compute and memory traffic, node-local detail mainly changes prefactors, while dense global covariance propagation changes the scaling class. Cross-scale models should therefore be judged by the intervention pathways and observables they preserve, validity domain, identifiability, empirical adequacy and cost. Receptor-aware mean fields are thus neither universal nor a mere realism-cost compromise, but a transparent, tractable strategy for selected mechanistic questions, provided each reduction step is independently validated.
item.dc:creator: Yannael Bossard, Lahna Bekri, Alain Destexhe

item.title: Structure is in the zoom: probing neural symmetry through dimensionality scaling
item.description: arXiv:2611.08506v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scaling exponents of neural dimensionality are read as properties of the code, and used to compare representations and benchmark models against cortex. Yet one recording of 11,311 mouse V1 neurons gives 0.25, 0.30 or 0.35, depending only on how it is subsampled. We show that such an exponent measures the population and the probe together. We split it exactly into a floor, which random subsets of the same sizes give, and a shift, which a declared axis of stimulus classes adds. The usual random-subsample exponent is almost all floor. Stimulus direction lifts the exponent in every grating recording by reading both symmetry sectors of the code: orientation, which repeats every half turn, and direction, which does not. The lift lives in trial-to-trial fluctuations that differ between directions, while the class means, which linear decoders read, pull it down. Two measured terms, how much the classes' fluctuations overlap and how the means sit against them, account for the shift. They give its sign where it changes: in Allen Neuropixels recordings, whose class means mostly raise the exponent, and in macaque V1. In an XY lattice whose classes stay on one orbit, temperature flips the sign as the two terms say, and in GPT-2 the shift ranks the indirect-object circuit's name-mover and backup heads. Reported with its path, its floor and its shift, an exponent says how much structure a probe finds and what carries it. Our open tool, rung, reports all three for any labelled neural recording or language-model layer: https://github.com/adilamin89/structure-in-the-zoom
item.dc:creator: Adil Amin

item.title: Learning Reusable Behavioral Motifs for Continuous Animal Behavior Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2506.15190v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Natural behavior evolves continuously and often reuses movement structure across contexts, but existing behavioral segmentation methods typically assign a single discrete syllable at each time point or impose restrictive generative assumptions. We introduce Motif-based Continuous Dynamics (MCD), a computational framework that models behavior as time-varying combinations of reusable behavioral motifs. MCD learns motifs as latent behavior-level features from transition dynamics, through spectral representation learning within a reinforcement learning framework. MCD then infers policies that combine these motifs across time or context, through offline imitation learning. This formulation avoids hard behavioral boundaries while capturing continuity and compositionality. Across simulated gridworld and continuous-control tasks, mouse maze navigation and pose data, MCD identifies reusable motifs that explain task and temporal variation. MCD therefore provides a flexible and interpretable framework for computational behavior analysis. Code is available in https://github.com/G1NO3/MCD.
item.dc:creator: Jiyi Wang, Jingyang Ke, Bo Dai, Anqi Wu

item.title: Geometry-aware similarity metrics for neural representations on Riemannian and statistical manifolds
item.description: arXiv:2603.28764v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Similarity measures such as centred kernel alignment (CKA) or representational similarity analysis (RSA) are widely used to compare the representational geometries employed by different neural networks to solve the same task. Yet, because existing methods compare the extrinsic geometry of representations in state space, rather than their intrinsic geometry, they may fail to capture subtle yet crucial distinctions between fundamentally different computations. Here, we introduce metric similarity analysis (MSA), a novel method which leverages tools from Riemannian geometry to compare the intrinsic geometry of neural representations under the manifold hypothesis. We show that MSA can be used to (i) disentangle neural computations of deep networks in rich vs. lazy learning regimes, (ii) compare the dynamics of recurrent neural networks and state-space models, and (iii) investigate the statistical manifolds of diffusion models. Overall, we introduce a mathematically grounded and broadly applicable framework to understand the mechanisms behind neural computations by contrasting their intrinsic geometries.
item.dc:creator: N Alex Cayco-Gajic, Arthur Pellegrino

item.title: Prospective Coding Improves Learning in Deep Continuous-Time Recurrent Networks
item.description: arXiv:2609.04134v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Temporal integration gives continuous-time recurrent networks memory, but in deep stacks it also delays bottom-up signals and attenuates top-down errors. We compensate for this delay by making each layer's bottom-up input prospective, and we develop Recursive Quadrature Filters (RQFs), biologically motivated temporal band-pass filters that are a special case of diagonal state-space models (SSMs). Starting from an energy model, we derive the RQF dynamics and show that each RQF is a band-pass filter whose learnable parameters control its tuning frequency and bandwidth. We then make each layer's bottom-up input prospective using a parameter-free two-tap update that leaves the recurrent transition and parallel scan unchanged. We extend this correction to general diagonal SSMs and show that it mitigates depth-dependent gradient attenuation when temporal gradients are truncated, i.e., spatial-only backpropagation. We evaluate the performance of RQFs, S5, and ORGaNICs (a nonlinear gated RNN with built-in attentional modulation and recurrent normalization) trained using full backpropagation through time (BPTT) and spatial-only backpropagation. Under full BPTT, the prospective variants of these models match or outperform their non-prospective controls in every configuration. A non-residual width-32 six-layer RQF achieves 96.09% accuracy on raw-audio Speech Commands with 31.9k parameters; a width-64 six-layer RQF achieves 83.36% on the 16,384-step Path-X task. We also introduce selective RQFs (sRQFs), which make each filter's input gain and, optionally, its bandwidth and tuning frequency input-dependent while retaining the parallel scan. With the input gain alone, the same six-layer model achieves 86.31% on Path-X; with all three input-dependent, a four-layer prospective sRQF solves Selective Copying (99.83%).
item.dc:creator: Shivang Rawat, Mirko Morello, Flaviano Morone, David J. Heeger

item.title: PINR-ESI: Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Implicit Neural Representation Framework for EEG Extended-Source Imaging
item.description: arXiv:2611.06700v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: EEG extended-source imaging aims to localize active cortical regions and characterize their spatial extent, yet supervised inverse networks typically depend on synthetic EEG-source pairs and may be sensitive to synthetic-to-real mismatch. We propose a physics-informed self-supervised implicit neural representation (INR) framework for spatial source reconstruction without paired source labels or simulation-based supervised pretraining. The lead field matrix encodes the source-to-sensor volume-conduction model and constrains the INR through agreement between predicted and measured EEG. Cortical current density is modeled as a continuous coordinate-conditioned field. A classical inverse estimate provides warm initialization and spatial constraints on source activity, while patch-integrated projection maps the field to discrete source coefficients for forward modeling. Simulations across varying noise levels, source extents, and source counts showed consistently low spatial dispersion and good localization performance. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations using real EEG recordings from epilepsy patients and intracranial stimulation experiments further supported the feasibility of the framework for source imaging. These findings suggest the potential of physics-informed self-supervised INR for extended-source imaging.
item.dc:creator: Zhiyong Zhou, Sheng Liao, Xiaolin Li, Youshen Xiao, Bin Dai, Surui Liu, Yakang Dai
